stops.name: Nola, the house below Cicala, birth and baptism
stops.campa: In the small Campanian city of Nola, under the shadow of Vesuvius and the lesser slope of Monte Cicala, a boy is born to Giovanni Bruno, a soldier of modest means, and Fraulisa Savolino, and is baptized Filippo. The volcano stands always in view, and the wide, fertile plain around the city, planted with vine and olive, will stay with him as the remembered ground of thought itself: he will speak of Nola again and again in the books written on the far side of the Alps, of the Thames and the Elbe, homesick for this one particular light.

stops.name: Naples, letters, logic, and dialectic
stops.campa: At about fourteen the boy is sent to Naples to study the humanities, logic, and dialectic, lodging and learning under the private tutors called il Sarnese and, above all, the Augustinian friar Teofilo da Vairano, who opens to him the arts of memory and the combinatory logic of Ramon Llull, the Catalan master dead two and a half centuries but newly urgent again. In Teofilo's rooms the boy first handles Llull's wheels of concepts turning within concepts, the seed of a method he will carry, transformed, through every court of Europe.

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore, the habit of the Order
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of July, seventeen years old, Filippo enters the great Dominican convent of San Domenico Maggiore as a novice cleric and takes, in religion, the name Giordano, after the Roman martyr of the Dominican calendar. Within these cloisters, once the school of Aquinas himself, he is given the full apparatus of scholastic philosophy and the freedom of a library stocked with condemned and half-condemned books. He conceals, against the order of the general chapter, a copy of the Fathers with the Erasmian annotations struck through by other hands but still legible beneath the strokes.

stops.name: Campagna, ordination and the first Mass at San Bartolomeo
stops.campa: Subdeacon, then deacon, Fra Giordano is consecrated priest once he has turned twenty-four, and is sent inland from Naples to say his first Mass in the Dominican house of San Bartolomeo at Campagna, above the Sele valley near Salerno. He is already remarked on: a memory that returns long passages after a single hearing, a tongue too quick for comfort in disputation. Earlier he has been sent to Rome to demonstrate his mnemonic art before Pope Pius V and Cardinal Rebiba, a brief public triumph that will not save him, for the same gift for saying exactly what he thinks is already collecting enemies inside the convent walls.

stops.name: Naples, the scholia of Erasmus and the heresy of Arius
stops.campa: Word reaches the Provincial that Fra Giordano has argued the Arian heresy against the Trinity in dispute with Fra Agostino da Montalcino, and has kept, against express prohibition, a copy of Chrysostom and Jerome with Erasmus's scholia scraped but not erased. A trial for heresy opens in Naples at the start of the year. Warned that arrest is coming, Giordano throws off the outward peace of the cloister he has worn for eleven years, sheds the white-and-black habit within weeks of the summons, and rides north before the Holy Office can close its hand on him.

stops.name: Rome, Santa Maria sopra Minerva, the habit set aside
stops.campa: He reaches Rome and asks shelter of his own order at the great Dominican house of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, still, technically, a friar in good standing outside Naples. But the Neapolitan file follows him north within weeks, thickened now with the report of a brother found drowned and old suspicion of foul play laid, unfairly or not, at his door. Giordano does not wait to be summoned a second time. He lays aside the white scapular of Saint Dominic for good, puts on the plain clothes of a wandering scholar, and turns north, a fugitive from his own vocation at twenty-eight.

stops.name: Noli, teaching grammar and the sphere for bread
stops.campa: Without habit, benefice, or protector, the ex-friar earns his keep as any masterless scholar must: at Noli on the Ligurian coast he teaches grammar to the town's boys for four months, and, for the local gentry curious about the heavens, gives lessons on Sacrobosco's sphere and the ordering of the planets. He will later tell his Venetian judges of these humble months plainly, without shame: a doctor of theology reduced to the schoolroom of children, and glad of the wage. From Noli he crosses to Savona, then inland to Turin, mapping in his own body the roads of an Italy too small now to hold him.
stops.quote: I went to Noli, on the Genoese riviera, and stayed there four months, teaching grammar to boys and reading the Sphere to certain gentlemen.
stops.quote_source: Venetian trial deposition, 1592 (Documenti del processo, ed. Firpo), in translation

stops.name: Venice, a small book on the signs of the times
stops.campa: The wandering scholar reaches Venice, city of presses free enough to print what Rome would burn, and has struck off a small treatise, De' segni de' tempi, on the signs and portents of the age: it does not survive, but its title alone marks a mind already reading the heavens as a text of prophecy and change rather than a fixed Aristotelian ceiling. He does not linger; the lagoon is a way-station, not a refuge, and within weeks he is on the road again westward, toward Padua and the university towns of the Veneto and Lombardy.

stops.name: Padua and Bergamo, the Dominicans who begged him back
stops.campa: At Padua, Dominican brothers of his own order recognize the fugitive and urge him to resume the habit and the observance, at least outwardly, the better to travel safely; he puts it on again for a season, a pragmatist's compromise, and lodges a while at Bergamo. But the compromise cannot hold a mind already loosed from every enclosure. Within the year he sheds the habit again, this time for good, and turns toward the mountains: Milan, then the Alpine passes, aiming for the Calvinist cantons where, whatever else awaits him, the Roman Inquisition's arm does not reach.

stops.name: Chambéry and the crossing into Geneva
stops.campa: He crosses by Chambéry in Savoy, resting briefly among monks who receive him as a curiosity more than a guest, and is advised by a French nobleman he meets on the road that a former friar traveling in his own habit through reformed country invites suspicion from both sides at once: better to go as a plain man. He takes the advice, and in the last months of the year passes the frontier into the Calvinist republic of Geneva, city of Calvin's memory and of presses that will, for a season, need a proofreader more than they need a confession of faith.

stops.name: Geneva, proofreader in Calvin's city
stops.campa: In Geneva, capital of a Reformation that is not his own, Giordano sets aside every outward mark of Rome, is received among the Italian exile congregation, and takes work correcting proof for the city's printers, the trade of many a displaced scholar. On the twentieth of May he matriculates at the Genevan Academy, entered in the rector's book as Filippo Bruno of Nola. For a few months it seems the fugitive might make a life here, among fellow Italians who fled the Inquisition before him: a proofreader's quiet, after three years on the road.

stops.name: Geneva, the pamphlet against La Faye, and the excommunication
stops.campa: His tongue betrays him again. Giordano has a broadsheet printed listing twenty errors he claims to find in a single lecture of Antoine de la Faye, professor of philosophy and pillar of the Calvinist Academy: it is read as defamation of a magistrate of the faith. On the thirteenth of August the consistory tries him and finds him guilty, all but excommunicate; after a weak defense he bends, confesses fault, and begs readmission to the sacrament. On the twenty-seventh he is absolved. But the episode leaves a scar of anti-Calvinist anger that will surface again and again in the books written after, and Geneva no longer wants him.
